profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a fintech market-surveillance startup after the latest weekly run of its signature-based anomaly detection pipeline produced a sharp drop in crypto pump-and-dump alerts and a noticeable rise in analyst-confirmed misses. The immediate context is that the team recently migrated randomized-signature feature extraction from a research notebook into the production batch workflow, and operations noticed that coins previously surfaced during known Telegram-coordinated spikes no longer appear near the top of the review queue. The agenda is to diagnose whether the regression comes from event slicing, feature generation, or post-feature scoring behavior, and to agree on a same-day corrective action before the next overnight run. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan and a patch path that both participants believe will return the detector to its prior behavior quickly enough for operations to trust tonight's alerts.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Alert review workflows, anomaly analysis, crypto market-abuse patterns, operational evaluation of detection systems
members.background: Former quantitative compliance analyst at a digital asset exchange who now owns analyst trust in the firm's surveillance alerts and translates research models into practical monitoring requirements for operations teams.
members.private_state: She needs alert quality to recover fast because operations has already escalated missed pump cases to leadership, and she wants a fix that restores analyst confidence without opening a longer debate about redesigning the detector.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the pre-migration baseline,' they mean the last pilot run before the production cutover, because that is the behavior analysts actually learned to trust.
A pump-detection 'window' naturally includes the buildup before the visible spike, since the coordinated accumulation pattern is what makes the case legible to reviewers.
If performance is 'restored,' the known missed Telegram-linked incidents from last week should reappear in the analyst queue, even if dashboard metrics are updated later.
Using 'the same randomized signature setup' means reproducing the same projection family and seed behavior from the trusted pilot so the resulting feature geometry is materially the same.
Feature-pipeline migrations are supposed to preserve review behavior unless someone explicitly changed event slicing or asset-universe filters.

members.name: Leo Werner
members.expertise: Time-series feature pipelines, productionization of research models, batch inference systems, reproducibility and compute optimization
members.background: Previously built production ML systems for market-data vendors and was hired to harden experimental quant models into reliable, scalable nightly jobs across large crypto transaction feeds.
members.private_state: He wants to contain the issue to an implementation detail rather than a broader architecture problem, and he is especially concerned about keeping the overnight batch within its compute budget after the migration.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the pre-migration baseline,' they mean the research configuration that the production migration was copied from, because that is the canonical source artifact for implementation parity.

An inference 'window' starts at the trigger timestamp and extends forward in a standardized slice, since production segmentation for detectors is defined around the scoring event rather than analyst review context.
If performance is 'restored,' aggregate validation metrics on the latest batch should return to their pre-migration range, even if the exact historical incidents surfaced are not identical.

Using 'the same randomized signature setup' means the same declared dimensionality and projection scheme; because the detector is unsupervised and refit on each batch, a different instantiated random seed is statistically equivalent and safe.
If a migration bug exists, it is most likely in implementation details of feature extraction rather than in the already-standardized batching and segmentation layer.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both compare the regressed run to 'the pre-migration baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the final pilot-operations run from May 28, the last run before cutover that analysts validated on the post-listing-filtered coin universe and event-centered review slices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the research backtest configuration from the model repository that served as the source artifact for the migration, which used the full tradable universe and standardized production segmentation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds more precise than plain 'baseline,' so both feel they are naming the same obvious reference point; Nina anchors on the last trusted operational run, while Leo anchors on the implementation source of the migration, and neither expects that distinction to matter enough to spell out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss checking or rebuilding the 'window' around suspicious activity.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means a 30-minute pre-spike plus 15-minute post-spike slice used by analysts to capture coordinated run-up behavior before the visible pump.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means a fixed 45-minute forward-looking inference slice starting at the trigger timestamp, because that is how production batch segmentation defines a scoring window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'window' is routine and both assume its alignment was settled long ago; the durations sound compatible enough that a normal troubleshooting exchange can proceed without anyone realizing one window is centered around buildup and the other begins only after the trigger.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to restore performance
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'restore performance' before tonight's run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the detector should again surface the specific analyst-reviewed pump incidents that were missed last week, so operations sees familiar case-level behavior return.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means batch-level precision, recall, or F1 on the current validation slice should return to the pre-migration range, even if the set of surfaced incidents shifts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both care about quality and use the same operational phrase, so the divergence between case-level recurrence and aggregate metric recovery feels too second-order to raise in a short, competent troubleshooting meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the same randomized signature setup
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both support 'using the same randomized signature setup' to get the pipeline back in line.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes this means reproducing the exact randomized projection behavior from the successful pilot run, including the specific seed path that made the extracted signatures effectively comparable to what analysts previously saw.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes this means keeping the same projection dimensionality, truncation level, and configuration template, while allowing production to instantiate a fresh shared projector seed per batch; because the anomaly detector is unsupervised and refit on-the-fly each batch, he believes seed changes are statistically equivalent and operationally safe.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'same setup' naturally sounds like enough detail for both sides: Nina hears behavioral sameness, while Leo hears parameter-level sameness; since the model is unsupervised rather than a fixed downstream classifier, his assumption remains plausible and does not obviously trigger a clarification.
